messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone,

I’m encountering a curious problem when running simulations for a very simple multistate capture recapture model. This model comprises three states: non-breeder, breeder, and dead. The transition probabilities are defined by survival (a single parameter) and breeding probability. Breeding probability is a function of an environmental covariate:

logit(beta[t]) = a1 + a2*env(t).

The parameters for the simulations yield CR datasets that should be more than large enough to estimate the parameters (25 occasions, 15 newly-marked individuals each year, p = 0.6, 1400 captures).

Yet for some reason the a2 parameter is systematically underestimated (in absolute value), regardless of whether it is positive or negative (e.g. relative bias is -8% when a2 = 1.2). All other parameters are estimated with a relative bias <1% (in absolute value).

Before simplifying the model, I noticed the same problem with other additive parameters. For instance, when including a cost of reproduction on breeding probability in an additive fashion:

logit(beta[1, t]) = a1 + a2*env(t)             for non-breeders

logit(beta[2, t]) = a1 + a2*env(t) + a3    for breeders

both a2 and a3 were underestimated (in absolute value).

I also noticed that the bias increases when the absolute value of a2 increases (e.g. bias is only -3% when a2 = 0.4, but -8% when a2 = 1.2), as well as when the quality of the datasets decreases.

I thought it might be an issue with my priors, but I’m using N(0, 10) for a2 (and N(0, 1.5) for a1). Also I expect that given the quality of the dataset, priors shouldn’t play too much of a role.

I’m fairly sure I haven’t made a mistake when simulating the data (I'm not simulating the data from the nimble model because I didn't manage to do so).

Does somebody have any idea what is going on here?

I attached the code used to create the datasets, to run the model, and to asses bias in parameter estimates.

Many thanks in advance,

Marwan

Hi, I'm trying to simulate data from a model following the example (https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/simulation_from_model.html). The example is much simpler than my case, so I may be misinterpreting how to deal with the many additional parameters in my model. In any case, it's not able to simulate the values I'm asking for (gives me all NAs). I'm wondering if this is because it's not finding all of the dependencies--some parameters seem to be missing from that list. My model runs correctly on real data, so it shouldn't be a problem with the model code itself. It could also be an issue with how I'm setting up constants/inits, because I'm not totally clear on how to do that when setting up to simulate data. I would very much appreciate any suggestions. Thank you!

Here's a reproducible example:

###############################

library(nimble)
set.seed(123)

# Set up sampling frame: 4 samples from each point in each year
nyrs <- 5
npts <- 20
trend <- -0.1 # ultimately this will be a power analysis to evaluate whether we can detect a trend in biomass over time, so here we set the annual change we want to simulate
simdatr <- as.data.frame(expand.grid(year=1:nyrs, point=1:npts, sample=1:4))

constants <- list(C=10000, zeros=rep(0,nrow(simdatr)),  # for zeros trick
## biological parameters:
# below, nimbleModel gives a note that it's using these as data, but is that right? My intent is to set these values (calculated from real data) as constant values to define how the simulated data are simulated.
b_yr=trend,
sd_eps=0.0944, sd_p=8.5500, sd_pt=1.1634,
alpha_h=5.4688,
alpha_b=3.9911,
r=2.9235, # I'm not certain whether I should specify r, but it didn't work without it either

## sampling frame:
nquads=nrow(simdatr),
npts=npts,
point=simdatr$point,
year=simdatr$year-mean(simdatr$year))

inits <- function () {list(
dat=runif(nrow(simdatr), 1,2),
b_pt=runif(npts,-1,1), # random effect of point on the biomass process
h_pt=runif(npts,-1,1) # random effect of point on the hurdle (occupancy) process
# I tried initializing these, but it said it was ignoring them when I provided the values above. If I provide the inits here and exclude them from constants, the simulation still returns NAs:
# alpha_h=runif(1,2,4), alpha_b=runif(1,4,6),
# b_yr=runif(1,-1,1),
# r=runif(1,1,2), sd_eps=runif(1,0,1),
# sd_pt=runif(1,0,1), sd_p=runif(1,0,1)
)}

## Set up the model. This is a Gamma hurdle model to estimate average annual biomass of eelgrass, where the hurdle is point-level occupancy and there are 4 samples taken at each point in each year.
mycode <- nimbleCode({

# intercepts and gamma shape params
alpha_h~dnorm(0,0.001)
alpha_b~dnorm(0,0.001)
r ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)

  # random point effects
for (o in 1:npts){
b_pt[o]~dnorm(alpha_b,tau_pt)
h_pt[o]~dnorm(alpha_h,tau_p)
}
tau_pt<-pow(sd_pt,-2)
sd_pt~dunif(0,10)
    tau_p<-pow(sd_p,-2)
    sd_p~dunif(0,10)

## year effect (continuous)
b_yr~dnorm(0,0.01)

# for every observation
for(i in 1:nquads){
# define the logistic regression model (hurdle), where w is the probability of occurrence.
# use the logistic transformation exp(z)/(1 + exp(z)), where z is a linear function
dat[i] ~ dgamma(sh[i], ra[i])
sh[i] <- pow(pred[i],2)/pow(pred_se[i],2)
ra[i] <-  pred[i]/pow(pred_se[i],2)
Y[i] <- dat[i]*z[i]
logit(w[i]) <- zeta[i]
zeta[i] <- h_pt[point[i]]

# define the gamma regression model for the mean (biomass). use the log link the ensure positive, non-zero mu
epsilon[i]~dnorm(0,tau_eps)
log(mu[i]) <- b_pt[point[i]]+ b_yr*year[i]  + epsilon[i] #

# gamma log-likelihood
lg1[i] <- - loggam(r) + r * log(r / mu[i])
lg2[i] <- (r - 1) * log(Y[i]+0.0000001) - (Y[i] * r) / mu[i] # add tiny value to prevent nimble from choking on log(0), even though the log(0) nodes aren't needed for anything
LG[i] <- lg1[i] + lg2[i]
l1[i] <- (1 - z[i]) * log(1 - w[i]) # note this is L-one
l2[i] <- z[i] * (log(w[i]) + LG[i])
ll[i] <- l1[i] + l2[i] # note this is LL
zeros[i] ~ dpois(-ll[i] + C)
}
tau_eps<-pow(sd_eps,-2)
sd_eps~dunif(0,2)

})

mymodel <- nimbleModel(mycode, constants=constants, inits=inits())
# Gives a note that it's using several inputs as data, but the simulation example didn't say anything about specifying data

# The values we want to simulate are pred and pred_se (these are the data values when we use this model on the real dataset), so get their dependencies:
nodesToSim <- mymodel$getDependencies(c('pred', 'pred_se'), self=F, downstream=T)
# this code is to concisely view what we're going to call with nodesToSim:
nts <- rep(NA, length(nodesToSim))
for(w in 1:length(nts)) nts[w] <- unlist(strsplit(nodesToSim[w],'[', fixed=TRUE))[1]
sort(unique(nts))
## This does not appear to include all of the dependencies; for example, shouldn't lg1 and l1 be shown here? Documentation for getDependencies() indicates nothing should be excluded by default.

mymodel$simulate(nodesToSim)
# gives a series of warnings:

# In rgamma(1, shape = model$sh[getNodeFunctionIndexedInfo(INDEXEDNODEINFO_,  ... :
#   NAs produced

mymodel$pred

One component of the model looks at the probability that a fish release on day i will be available to recapture on day j, this is done through a discretized distribution function of lognormal distribution.

messages.body_plain:
hi Emily,

I think there may be a mismatch between how you are thinking about your problem and how we think about nimble models.

For a simulation, we'd expect that you want to simulate data values. Data are stochastic nodes that have no dependencies and that are observed/measured.
The distribution(s) of the data nodes determines the likelihood for the model. You seem to say that `dat` is data but then that `pred` and `pred_se` are data.

In your code, `pred` and `pred_si` appear only on the right hand side of declarations. They are not assigned a distribution (and are not defined deterministically) so nimble has no way to simulate into `pred` and `pred_si` (though you are free to set values for `pred` and `pred_si` via constants, data, or inits). Similarly, `z` is never defined on the left hand side of a declaration.

I'm not sure it will help but let's consider a simple regression case.

for(i in 1:n)
 y[i] ~ dnorm(b0 + b1*x[i], 1)
b0 ~ dnorm(0, 1)
b1 ~ dnorm(0, 1)

In that case, we can simulate values of b0, b1, and the y's (or you might choose not to simulate b0 and b1 and just fix at reasonable values). We cannot simulate (in nimble) values of x[i] because x[i] has no distribution assigned to it.
You might think of both `y` and `x` as being data (and can be assigned values with the `data` argument), but with nimble, the y's here are data nodes,
while the x's are "right-hand-side only" nodes.

Now in a simulation, it could make sense to simulate values of `x`. But you wouldn't be able to do that with the nimble model as given. You'd have to do it in R and then
put values for x into the model. Alternatively you could give `x` priors for the purpose of simulation but for the purpose of fitting the model make sure to provide values for `x`
via data so MCMC sampling is not done for `x`.

I haven't delved into the question of what `getDependencies` is doing here because I wanted to get a better understanding of what you are trying to do first.

I'll also say that there are cases where one might have data defined deterministically such as the latent variable representation of probit regression. I'm not sure if that is relevant here.

-chris

Hi Frédéric,

If you are wanting to calculate WAIC from a saved set of samples, then you're right that you need to run the `calculateWAIC` function. And for that you need to save all parameters needed for the WAIC calculation (generally stochastic parents of data nodes, but not stochastic parents of those parents).

The `calculateWAIC` method of the MCMC object is an internal method not intended for use by users and (I hope) not documented anywhere as being something users would use.

I don't think I will try to recover/interpret the history of the whole discussion unless it ends up being important. I suspect that when we were responding to Michael we overlooked a chunk of code that is not what one would want to use.

messages.subject_clean: How to fit mixed effect model in NIMBLE
messages.body_plain:
Jun, thanks for your question, and your use of nimble.

As the warning message suggests (" [Warning] Multiple definitions for the same node.  Did you forget indexing with 'i' on the left-hand side of   `M[j] ~ dnorm ...."), the issue you're encountering is that the declaration for M[j] is enclosed (not only inside the loop over j, but also) inside the loop over i.  So, for each pair of values {i,j}, nimble attempts to create a "new" node in the model defined by M[j].  However, if i takes on multiple values, this results in (attempting to) create M[j] multiple times, which is not allowed.

This can be fixed, but adding indexing over i as well, for the EM and M variables:

for(i in 1:N) {

# for i th subject
# they may have different number of clustered observations

    for(j in s[i]:e[i]) {
      EM[i,j] <- (beta[L[i], 1]) + Time[j]*beta[L[i], 2] + b0[i] * sigma_b
      M[i,j] ~ dnorm(EM[i,j], sd = sigma_M)
    }
  }

Assuming everything else with your model is correct (priors, the specification of Time, L, etc), this should hopefully get you going.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Re: Any way to deal with label switching in latent class modeling
messages.subject_clean: Any way to deal with label switching in latent class modeling
messages.body_plain:
Jun, thanks again for your question, and your use of nimble.

The exact approach to preventing label-switching might depend on your model itself.  However, if each latent class has a parameter specific to it, for example a group-specific mean parameter, then you can prevent label switching by imposing an ordering over the group-specific means.  For example, if you have 2 groups, with means mu[1] and mu[2], then you can impose the ordering mu[1] < mu[2] using the dconstraint distribution by including the following line in your model code:

code <- nimbleCode({
   ...
   one ~ dconstraint(mu[1] < mu[2])
})

then also supplying the value one = 1 in your "data" list argument to nimbleModel:

data <- list(...., one = 1)
model <- nimbleModel(code, ..., data = data)

There are certainly other more complex cases, but this sort of approach can usually be used to prevent label switching between groups.

I hope this gets you going, but feel free to be more specific with your model if a more specific answer would be helpful.

Cheers,
Daniel

Hi Jacob,

Thanks for the question. From reading your code, I think you need to do "sig=double(1)" in the definition of "g". (BTW, this is described in help(nimIntegrate), in the details about the function argument ("f" there)). The reason it needs to be a vector is that for compilation purposes nimble has stricter argument and type requirements than R, and a vector provides a way to allow the function argument to take as much information as one needs. Then you'll want to replace "sig" by "sig[1]" in the equation. You can still use  "fx <- nimIntegrate(g, lower = 0, upper = 150, param = sig)" even though sig is a scalar here. In the specific situation, nimble will arrange to convert sig to a vector of length 1.

I want to clarify what I think you might mean by running in vs out of nimbleMCMC. I'm not 100% sure but I think you might actually be talking about running compiled vs uncompiled. It is possible to build and compile the steps of a model and MCMC algorithm outside of nimbleMCMC. I believe in that case you would still encounter the error you saw. On the other hand it is possible to use a model or MCMC algorithm uncompiled. In that case, the additional run-time type flexibility of R allows some situations to run fine even though they will fail to compile. Please let me know if that does not sound right.

HTH
Perry

Hi Colton, Perry,

A little late to the party, but I'm trying to do a similar thing (using an Rcpp fn in nimble). One note that might be helpful:  if you make a package out of your rcpp function this will generate the .o file for you (you will have to make the header file, but that is straight forward).  It might seem daunting to create a package from an rcpp file (or files), but it is actually pretty simple thanks to some rcpp functionality; there are built in functions to create the package file structure, and to build the package once the .cpp/.h files are added to the source folder.  A couple of links with info on building packages:

> Hi Colton,
> For quick answers:
> 1. Look at nimbleExternalCall. It is somewhat rudimentary but is designed to let you call C/C++ code directly (from compiled nimble code), without going through the R interpreter. But to use Rcpp, you may have to code the C++ and create the #includes etc yourself and rely less on Rcpp's slickness (e.g. sourceCpp) directly from R. You need to have access to both the .o and .h files.
> 2. I am not a deSolve expert but I think it wraps layers of R processing around a call to a C++ internal that does the actual integration. It may be the case that all the time in the R interpreter is what is so costly. If nimbleExternalCall is too clunky, you could do the following: Use Rcpp completely independently of nimble, so that you have an R function (created by Rcpp) that calls directly to compiled code to compute what you want. Then call that function via a nimbleRcall. The overhead for the nimbleRcall should be much less (but not nothing) if you're not spending time executing R other than calling back into compiled code.
> I'm happy to help look at details or sketch ideas if you start exploring one of these.
> HTH
